nameStory: The Common Spitting Spider earned its dramatic name from its unique hunting technique — it literally spits at its prey! When it spots a meal, this tiny spider shoots a zigzag pattern of sticky, venomous silk from special glands in its front body section. This gooey projectile pins down insects instantly, making the spider a miniature web-slinger with deadly accuracy.
description: The Common Spitting Spider is a tiny house spider with a distinctive hunchbacked appearance that sets it apart from other spiders. Growing only 3-6 millimeters long (about the size of a pencil eraser), it has an unusual body shape where the front section slopes upward like a tiny hill while the back section slopes downward. Unlike most spiders that have eight eyes, this species has just six eyes arranged in three pairs, giving it a unique facial structure that spider enthusiasts find fascinating.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The front section (cephalothorax) slopes dramatically upward toward the back while the abdomen slopes downward, creating a distinctive hunchbacked or camel-like profile that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Has only six eyes instead of the typical eight, arranged in three pairs that create a triangular pattern when viewed from the front

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny spider measuring just 3-6 millimeters, small enough to sit comfortably on a dime with room to spare

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves very slowly and deliberately, and when hunting, extends its front legs and sways slightly before spitting at prey — no web building observed

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build webs for catching prey; instead uses its silk-spitting ability to hunt, though may create simple silk retreats in crevices

habitat: Common Spitting Spiders prefer the warm, dry spaces inside New England homes, particularly in basements, closets, and behind furniture where they hunt for small insects. They're also found in barns, sheds, and other protected structures, typically hiding in cracks and crevices during the day. Outdoors, look for them under loose bark, in rock crevices, or in other sheltered spots that stay relatively dry.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots in basements and protected areas. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving slowly across walls or floors indoors.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when hunting behavior is most easily observed. Adults are reproducing and can occasionally be found with egg sacs in their hiding places.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting as they prepare for winter, often moving deeper into buildings. Young spiders may be seen dispersing to find their own territories.
seasonality.winter: Become much less active and retreat to protected spaces like basement crevices, wall voids, or under stored items where they remain relatively dormant until spring.

funFact: This spider has silk glands in both the front and back of its body — the front ones are connected to its venom glands to create toxic silk bullets that it can accurately shoot up to 10 times its own body length, making it one of nature's tiniest snipers!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small house spiders, but the distinctive hunchbacked profile makes identification easy — remember "spitting spider, sloping silhouette" and look for that unusual upward-sloping front section that no other common house spider has.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their dramatic name and spitting ability, these spiders are completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial as they hunt pest insects like flies and mosquitoes. The "spitting" behavior is fascinating to observe but requires patience since these spiders move very slowly and may take several minutes to position themselves before shooting.
compareHints: The Common Spitting Spider differs from its relative the Brown Spitting Spider primarily in coloration and markings, though both share the characteristic hunchbacked body shape and six-eye arrangement. Brown Spitting Spiders tend to be darker overall with less distinct patterning, while Common Spitting Spiders typically show more varied coloration with subtle patterns on their bodies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Brown Spitting Spider differs from the Common Spitting Spider mainly in coloration - it's much darker and more uniformly brown, lacking the lighter background with distinctive dark patterns typical of its relative.
